# From Avestan to canonical spelling: the journey of VohuManah

Long before it became a digital address, ​this name travelled through scripts. **VohuManah** begins in Avestan, passes through scholarly transliteration, and arrives in a Latin form that needs no special encoding. Each stage preserves some information and requires some ‌judgment. This post follows that journey: the original evidence, the reconstructed pronunciation, the mythological record, the material remains, and the reviewed spelling used by the temple.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** VohuManah
- ‌**ASCII form:** vohumanah
- **Meaning:** "Good thought"
- **Domain of influence:** Good Mind, Cattle
- **Pantheon:** Zoroastrian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form
- **Original script:** 𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵 (Avestan)

## Overview

**VohuManah** (*vohumanah*) — Good Mind, Cattle · Good thought ​— belongs to the Zoroastrian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Good Mind, Cattle". The name means "Good thought".

**VohuManah** — Good Mind, Good Purpose — is the first of the ​six Amesha Spentas, the Holy Immortals who surround Ahura Mazdā. He is the thought that chooses truth before word and deed, the guardian of cattle and patient prosperity, and the divine visitor ​who appeared to Zarathuštra on the river Dāitya to open the way to revelation.

PuniCodex records the canonical scholarly spelling **VohuManah** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/vohumanah/). The displayed form is ​ASCII-equivalent — a description computed from the displayed form itself. The plain ASCII form *vohumanah* contains the same letters: no recovered diacritics or special encoding is claimed. The work here is consistent citation, ​capitalization, provenance, and cultural context.

## The Original Script

The name is preserved in Avestan as **𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵**.

The scholarly transliteration is *Vohu Manah*.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- Vohu Manah is one ​of the Amesha Spentas praised in the Gathas.
- The final -h in Vohu and Manah represents Avestan h (𐬵).
- The vowel o in Vohu is written with the Avestan letter o (𐬊).

## Mythology

The stories of VohuManah place good mind, cattle at the center of a ​living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

VohuManah appears in zoroastrian tradition as good mind, cattle. The name's meaning, "Good thought", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees and later ​tradition-keepers preserved VohuManah in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of VohuManah survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version reflects the ​interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. The restoration VohuManah ​gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### The Soul of the Bull (Yasna 29)

The Gāthās' strangest litigant is cattle. 'The soul of the bull came to you, ‌O Wise One, lamenting' — the lament asks for whom the herds were shaped and who will protect them from violence and ill care (Yasna 29.1, 9). Against the raider and the careless ​master, the soul of the ox — emblem of every creature that feeds and works for us — demands an advocate, and the divine council deliberates with the Good Mind, promising a ‌prophet who will teach protection through Vohu Manah (Yasna 29.7–10). Later tradition assigns him the guardianship of cattle explicitly, and the bull becomes his living emblem. The lawsuit never closes: the herd's ​welfare remains the standing test of every settlement. **Zoroastrian ethics begins with the weakest plaintiff — a voiceless animal — and its first commandment is husbandry: the good mind is the mind ‌that keeps the herd alive**.

### The Two Minds (Yasna 30)

'Now the two spirits, in the beginning the twins, renowned to be in conflict' (Yasna 30.3). One, the Bounteous, chose truth as the ​wise masters do; but the other refused, and through the fury of violence the worst mind, *akəm manō*, rushed upon mortals (Yasna 30.4–6). Thus Aka Manah — Bad Mind — is born ‌as Vohu Manah's twin and shadow, and every human skull becomes the battlefield where the two contend for attention. The myth reads like psychology before the word existed: the origin of evil ​is located not in matter, not in fate, but in mentality — a choice of orientation made at the beginning and repeated in every waking hour. **Evil is not an invading army but ‌a way of thinking, and goodness likewise — moral life begins as a mental choice repeated daily**.

### The Vision on the River Dāitya (Dēnkard 7)

The Pahlavi Dēnkard (Book 7) preserves the ​great theophany. Zarathuštra, mocked by the sacrificial guilds, withdraws to the ford of the river Dāitya — and there Vohu Manah appears to him in a form of light, come to open ​the way: bring your questions before the Creator, he says, and the dialogue that becomes the Gāthās begins. The vision sets the pattern of Zoroastrian revelation: the Good Mind is the doorkeeper ‌of wisdom; prayer must be intelligent before it is fervent, and the seeker's disposition is part of the revelation's equipment. Later tradition made Vahman the first of the four Amahraspands set around Ohrmazd ‌and the guardian of the first watch of day. The pattern became doctrine: in the daily round, Vahman's hour is the first watch of morning, and prayer begins where he appeared. **Before ‌any angel appears, the seeker must be mentally prepared — theophany rewards the disciplined mind**.

The iconography associated with VohuManah concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each ​a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form VohuManah, carrying scholarly and cultural weight.
- **Domain** — Good Mind, Cattle

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and ​artists to recognize VohuManah across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling VohuManah carries the same precision ‌in textual form.

- **The bull** — The soul of the ox whose complaint opens the Gāthās' ethics; cattle are his charge (Yasna 29)
- **The good word** — Thought made speech: the middle ​term of the triad good thought, good word, good deed
- **The garment of light** — In Zarathuštra's vision Vahman appears as a figure of light on the river Dāitya (Dēnkard, Book 7)
- ​**Bahman, the eleventh month** — His Middle Persian name as a living calendar dedication and the feast Bahmanagān

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus is yet ‌assigned to VohuManah with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Zoroastrian name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary evidence remains the ​textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming 𐬬𐬊𐬵𐬎 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬵, sanctuary or cult remains tied to good ​mind and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**VohuManah** is ‌good mind, cattle. The name means "Good thought" and belongs to the zoroastrian tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration VohuManah returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### Good Mind

Central domain: good mind, cattle.

### Living ​Tradition

Honored in zoroastrian myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Canonical Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple with its canonical scholarly spelling and supporting evidence.

### The First Immortal

First of the Amesha Spentas ‌invoked in every Yasna — the thought that chooses Aša before word and deed (Yasna 1.12).

### Guardian of Cattle

Charged with the soul of the bull and the herds — the slow, ​patient goods of a well-kept world (Yasna 29).

### The Two Minds

Opposed at creation by Aka Manah, Bad Mind — the twin and shadow he has fought ever since (Yasna 30.4–6).

### Bahman, ​the Eleventh Month

His Middle Persian name Vahman lives in the calendar: the month Bahman, its day dedications, and the feast Bahmanagān.

## A Meditation

Cattle are the clue. Vohu Manah's charge is not ​intellect but the slow, warm, patient goods: herds, harvests, the long prosperity of a well-kept household. The Good Mind is the mindset of the good shepherd — unhurried, watchful, kind to what feeds ​us. Against it stands Aka Manah, the mind that is clever, quick, and ruinous. The pair maps uncomfortably well onto our own economy of attention: the feed engineered to be bad for ‌us is a cattle-drive run by Aka Manah. Zarathuštra's question — whose mind are you thinking with? — is four millennia old and still the diagnostic question of a life.
